This kind of speech indicates the utmost glorification of the Qur'an, just as a man may say, when he wishes to exalt a person from whom he needs something: "I seek your intercession with yourself, and I swear by your right over you."

The fourth issue: ﴿al-Mubin﴾ (the Clear) is that which includes the explanation of what people need in their religion and their worldly affairs. He described it as "making clear," although the true act of making clear belongs to God, because the clarification was achieved through it, as He said: ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an relates to the Children of Israel﴾ [al-Naml: 76], and He said in another verse: ﴿We relate to you the best of stories﴾ [Yusuf: 3], and He said: ﴿Or have We sent down to them an authority, so that it speaks of what they used to associate?﴾ [al-Rum: 35]. Thus He described it with speech, since it is the utmost in clarification, so it is as though it were a tongue that speaks; and the purpose in this is to exaggerate its description with this meaning.

The fifth issue: They differed concerning this blessed night. Most said it is the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr). ʿIkrimah and another group said it is the Night of Acquittal (Laylat al-Bara'a), which is the night of the middle of Sha'ban. As for the first group, they argued for the soundness of their view with several points:
The first: He said: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Power﴾ [al-Qadr: 1], and here He said: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during a blessed night﴾. So it must be that this blessed night is that which is called the Night of Power, lest there be contradiction.
The second: He said: ﴿The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was sent down﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185], thus clarifying that the sending down of the Qur'an occurred in the month of Ramadan; and here He said: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during a blessed night﴾. So this blessed night must fall in the month of Ramadan, and everyone who said this blessed night falls in Ramadan said it is the Night of Power; thus it is established that it is the Night of Power.
The third: He said describing the Night of Power: ﴿The angels and the Spirit descend therein by permission of their Lord, concerning every matter﴾ ﴿Peace it is﴾ [al-Qadr: 4–5]. He also said here: ﴿In it every wise matter is made distinct﴾, which is appropriate to His saying: ﴿The angels and the Spirit descend therein﴾ [al-Qadr: 4]. Here He said: ﴿a command from Us﴾, and in that verse He said: ﴿by permission of their Lord concerning every matter﴾ [al-Qadr: 4]. Here He said: ﴿as a mercy from your Lord﴾, and in that verse He said: ﴿Peace it is﴾ [al-Qadr: 5]. When the descriptions are close, it is necessary to say that one of the two nights is the other.
The fourth: Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari narrated in his Tafsir from Qatadah that he said: "The scrolls of Ibrahim were sent down on the first night of Ramadan, the Torah on the sixth night of it, the Psalms on the twelfth night that had passed of it, the Gospel on the eighteenth night that had passed of it, and the Qur'an on the twenty-fourth night that had passed of Ramadan; and the blessed night is the Night of Power."
The fifth: The Night of Power was named so because its worth (qadr) and nobility with God is great. It is known that its worth and nobility are not due to that time itself, because time is one thing in its essence and attributes, so it is impossible for some part of it to be more noble than another in its essence. Thus it is established that its nobility and worth are due to the fact that great noble matters occurred in it, which have great worth and a lofty rank. It is known that the rank of religion is higher and greater than the rank of this world, and the highest and most noble of things in religion in rank is the Qur'an, because through it the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ was established, and through it the distinction between truth and falsehood became manifest in all the other revealed books of God, as He said describing it: ("and a guardian over it" [al-Ma'idah: 48]), and through it the degrees of the people of felicity and the depths of the people of wretchedness became manifest. Accordingly, nothing is greater in worth, higher in mention, or greater in rank than the Qur'an. So if its descent had occurred in another night besides the Night of Power, then the Night of Power would be this second night, not the first. And since they agreed that the Night of Power which falls in Ramadan is the one, we know that the Qur'an was sent down in that night.

As for those who say that the blessed night mentioned in this verse is the middle night of Sha'ban, I have not seen for them any proof to rely upon; they have been content merely to transmit it from some people. If there is a saying from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ concerning it, then there is nothing more to be said; otherwise the truth is the first view. Then these proponents of this view claim that the middle night of Sha'ban has four names: the Blessed Night, the Night of Acquittal, the Night of the Decree (Laylat al-Sakk), and the Night of Mercy. It is also said that it was named the Night of Acquittal and the Night of the Decree because when the official (bunduar) collects the land tax from its people, he writes them an acquittal; likewise, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, writes an acquittal for His believing servants on this night. It is also said: this night is specific to five qualities:
The first: the distinguishing of every wise matter therein, as He said: ﴿In it every wise matter is made distinct﴾.
The second: the excellence of worship in it. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever prays one hundred units of prayer on this night, Allah sends to him one hundred angels: thirty to give him good news of Paradise, thirty to secure him from the punishment of the Fire, thirty to ward off the calamities of this world, and ten to ward off the schemes of Satan."
The third quality: the descent of mercy. He, peace be upon him, said: "Indeed Allah shows mercy to my community on this night in number equal to the hair of the sheep of the Banu Kalb."
The fourth quality: the attainment of forgiveness. He ﷺ said: "Indeed Allah, Exalted, forgives all Muslims on that night, except a soothsayer, or a person harboring enmity, or a habitual drinker of wine, or one who is disobedient to his parents, or one who persists in fornication."
The fifth quality: that God gave His Messenger on this night the complete intercession. That is, he asked on the thirteenth night of Sha'ban for his community, and was given a third of it; then he asked on the fourteenth night and was given two-thirds; then he asked on the fifteenth night and was given all of it, except whoever fled from God as a camel flees.
I have transmitted this section from the *Kashshaf*. If it is said: there is no doubt that time is an expression for the extended duration whose measure is the motions of the spheres and the stars, and that in itself it is a thing whose parts are alike, so it is impossible for some of its parts to be better than others; and place is an expression for extended space and empty void, so it is impossible for some of its parts to be more noble than others; and if that is so, then specifying some of its parts with greater nobility over the rest is a preference of one side of a possibility over the other without a determining cause, and that is impossible. We say: the affirmation of the createdness of the world and the affirmation that its Agent is a free-choosing agent is based on this principle, namely that it is not improbable for a free-choosing agent to specify a particular time for bringing the world into being rather than what precedes or follows it. If this principle is refuted, then the createdness of the world is refuted and the free-choosing Agent is refuted, and then the discussion of the interpretation of the Qur'an would have no benefit. And if this principle is sound, then the question you raised is removed. This is the reliable answer. People have also said: it is not improbable that God specifies some times with greater honor, so that this becomes an incentive for the responsible person to undertake acts of obedience in that time. For this reason He made it clear that He concealed it among the times and did not specify it; for if it were not specific, the responsible person would suppose in every time that it might be that noble time, and this would move him to persist in acts of obedience at all times. When you reflect on this principle, it becomes clear to you that time and place only gained additional distinctions following the nobility of the human being, who is the principal, and everything else is subordinate to him. And God knows best.

The sixth issue: It is narrated that ʿAṭiyyah al-Ḥarūrī asked Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, about His saying: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Power﴾ [al-Qadr: 1] and His saying: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during a blessed night﴾, how is this valid, given that Allah sent down the Qur'an in all the months? Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: "O son of the black woman, if I die and this comes into your mind and you do not find its answer, you are ruined. The Qur'an descended all at once from the Preserved Tablet to the House of Honor (al-Bayt al-Ma'mur), which is in the lowest heaven; then it descended afterward in various events, occasion by occasion." And God knows best.

The seventh issue: explaining the arrangement of these verses. Know that their purpose is the glorification of the Qur'an from three aspects:
The first: the explanation of the glorification of the Qur'an in terms of its own essence.
The second: the explanation of its glorification by reason of the nobility of the time in which it was sent down.

The third aspect: the explanation of its greatness in terms of the nobility of its rank.

As for the explanation of its greatness in terms of its essence, it has three aspects:

The first is that God Most High swore by it, and that indicates its nobility.

The second is that God Most High swore by it regarding its being sent down on a blessed night. We have mentioned that swearing by a thing with regard to one of its own states indicates that it is at the utmost level of nobility.

The third is that God Most High described it as being "clear" (mubin), and that also indicates its nobility in its essence.

As for the second type, which is the explanation of its nobility by virtue of the nobility of the time at which it was sent down, it is His saying: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down on a blessed night﴾. This is an alert that its being sent down on a blessed night requires its nobility and majesty. Then we say: His saying ﴿Indeed, We sent it down on a blessed night﴾ requires two matters. One is that God Most High sent it down. The second is that this night is blessed. God then mentioned, after this statement, what serves as an explanation of each of the two. As for the explanation of why God Most High sent it down, it is His saying: ﴿Indeed We were ever warners﴾, meaning that the wisdom in sending down this sura is that the warning of creation is not complete except by it. As for the explanation that this night is a blessed night, there are two matters. One is that God Most High makes every wise matter distinct therein. The second is that this wise matter is distinguished by the nobility that it manifests only from His presence, and to this is the allusion in His saying: ﴿a command from Us﴾.

As for the third type, it is the explanation of the nobility of the Qur'an by virtue of the nobility of its Sender. This is His saying: ﴿Indeed We were ever senders﴾. He thus explained that this warning and sending were brought about only by God Most High. Then He explained that this sending was for the sake of perfecting mercy, which is His saying: ﴿as a mercy from your Lord﴾. The expected phrasing would have been "as a mercy from Us," but He placed the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun, to signify that lordship (rububiyyah) requires mercy upon those who are nurtured. Then He explained that this mercy fell in accordance with the needs of those in need, because God Most High hears their supplications and knows the kinds of their needs. Therefore He said: ﴿Indeed He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾. This is what came to mind regarding how some of these verses are connected to others.

**Eighth issue: explaining the individual words of these expressions.**

As for His saying Most High: ﴿Indeed We sent it down on a blessed night﴾, it has been said regarding it that God Most High sent down the Qur'an in its entirety from the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz) to the lowest heaven on this night, and then He sent down at every time what the responsible person needs. It has also been said: the copying of that from the Preserved Tablet begins on the Night of Acquittal (laylat al-bara'ah), and the completion takes place on the Night of Decree (laylat al-qadr). Then the copy of provisions is handed to Mika'il, the copy of wars to Jibril, likewise earthquakes, thunderbolts and landslides, the copy of deeds to Isma'il, the lord of the lowest heaven, who is a great angel, and the copy of calamities to the Angel of Death.

Page 206

As for His saying Most High: ﴿wherein every wise matter is made distinct﴾, meaning, on that blessed night every wise matter is made distinct, that is, it is detailed and clarified, from their saying: "I separated the thing, I separate it, separation (farq) and criterion (furqan)." The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari's commentary) said: it is read as yufarriqu with shaddah, and as yafruqu with the verb ascribed to the agent and kull in the accusative. The one who distinguishes is God, Mighty and Majestic. Zayd ibn Ali read nufarriqu with the nun.

As for His saying: ﴿every wise matter﴾, al-hakim means "possessor of wisdom." This is because God Most High's assigning each person a specific state in terms of lifespan, provision, term, happiness and misery indicates His profound wisdom. Since those acts and decrees indicate the wisdom of their Doer, they are described as wise. This is a metaphorical attribution, because "wise" is in reality an attribute of the one who issues the command, and describing the matter as such is figurative. Then He said: ﴿a command from Us﴾. Regarding the accusative case of His saying ﴿amran﴾ there are two possibilities.

The first is that it is in the accusative by way of specification (ikhtisas). This is because God Most High explained the nobility of those decrees and rulings by describing them as wise, and then increased the explanation of their nobility by saying: "I mean by this matter a matter arising from Us, existing from Our presence, as Our knowledge and governance require."

The second is that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), and in this there are three possibilities:

The first is that it is a circumstantial state of one of the two pronouns in ﴿We sent it down﴾: either of the pronoun of the agent, meaning ﴿Indeed We sent it down﴾ issuing commands with a command, or of the pronoun of the object, meaning ﴿Indeed We sent it down﴾ while it is a command from Us with what must be done.

The third is what Abu Ali al-Farisi related from Abu al-Hasan, may God have mercy on them both: that he took His saying ﴿amran﴾ as a circumstantial state, and the qualified noun (dhu al-hal) is His saying ﴿every wise matter﴾, which is indefinite.

\* \* \*

Then He said: ﴿Indeed We were ever senders﴾, meaning: indeed We performed that warning only for the sake of "Indeed We were ever senders," meaning the prophets.

\* \* \*

Then He said: ﴿as a mercy from your Lord﴾, meaning, for the sake of mercy, so it is in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu).

\* \* \*

Then He said: ﴿Indeed He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾, meaning that this mercy was truly mercy, because those in need either mention their needs with their tongues or do not mention them. If they mention them, He Most High hears their speech and so knows their needs; and if they do not mention them, He Most High knows them. Thus it is established that His being (All-Hearing, All-Knowing) requires that He send down His mercy upon them.

\* \* \*

Then He said: ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, if you are certain﴾. There are issues regarding this:

The first issue: Ibn Amir... — *[see note below]*

The first issue: Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "rabbi" with a kasrah on the ba' as an adjunct to His saying ﴿as a mercy from your Lord﴾, while the rest read it with a dammah as an adjunct to His saying ﴿He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾.

The second issue: the purpose of this verse is that when the one who sends down is described with this majesty and greatness, what is sent down, which is the Qur'an, is at the utmost level of nobility and elevation.

The third issue: the benefit of His saying ﴿if you are certain﴾ is of several aspects:

The first: Abu Muslim said: its meaning is, if you seek certainty and desire it, then know that the matter is as We have said, like their saying: "So-and-so is a man of Najd and Tihamah," meaning he intends Najd and Tihamah.

The second: the author of al-Kashshaf said: they used to acknowledge that the heavens and the earth had a Lord and Creator, so it was said to them: the sending of messengers and the sending down of books is a mercy from the Lord, glory be to Him and exalted, then it was said: this is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing, whom you acknowledge and admit to be the Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, if your acknowledgment is from knowledge and certainty, just as you say: "This is the bounty of Zayd, whose generosity people have heard of, if his report has reached you and you have heard his story." Then He Most High rejected that they were certain, by His saying: ﴿Nay, but they are in doubt, playing﴾, and that their acknowledgment does not proceed from knowledge and certainty, nor from earnestness and reality, but is a statement mixed with mockery and play. And God knows best.

The Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 44, verses 10–16:

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So watch for the day when the sky brings a clear smoke﴾ ﴿covering the people. This is a painful punishment﴾ ﴿Our Lord, remove the punishment from us; indeed we are believers﴾ ﴿How will they have the reminder, when a clear messenger has already come to them?﴾ ﴿Then they turned away from him and said, "A taught one, a madman."﴾ ﴿Indeed We will remove the punishment a little, but you will surely return﴾ ﴿on the day We seize with the greatest seizing; indeed We will take vengeance.﴾

Know that what is meant by His words ﴿watch﴾ (ارتقب) is "wait," and this word is used for what is disliked. The meaning is: wait, O Muhammad, for their punishment. The object of "waiting" (الارتقاب) has been omitted, because what follows indicates it, namely His words ﴿This is a painful punishment﴾. It is also permissible that ﴿the day when the sky brings﴾ be the object of "waiting." As for His words ﴿with smoke﴾, there are two opinions:

The first opinion: The Prophet ﷺ prayed against his people in Mecca when they denied him, and he said: "O Allah, make their years like the years of Joseph." So the rain stopped, the earth became barren, and hunger struck the Quraysh so severely that they ate bones, dogs and carrion. A man, because of the hunger he suffered, would see between himself and the sky something like smoke. This is the view of Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, in some narrations, and of Muqatil and Mujahid, and it is the choice of al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj. It is also the view of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, who denied that the smoke could be anything other than this, which afflicted them from the severity of hunger, a darkness in their sight, so that they seemed to see smoke. The conclusion is that this smoke is the darkness in their eyes caused by the severity of hunger. Ibn Qutayba mentioned two ways of explaining the smoke as this condition:

First: In a year of drought, the dryness of the earth greatly increases because the rain has stopped; dust rises in great quantity and the air darkens. This resembles smoke, and for this reason a year of famine is called "the dusty" (al-ghabra').

Second: The Arabs call an overwhelming evil "smoke," so one says: "There was a matter between us from which smoke rose." The reason is that when a person's fear or weakness becomes intense, his eyes darken, and he sees the world as if it were filled with smoke.

The second opinion about the smoke is that it is a smoke that appears in the world and is one of the signs of the Resurrection. They said: When this condition occurs, the believers experience something like a cold in the head, and the disbelievers experience a state in which their heads become like the head of a roasted animal. This view is transmitted from Ali ibn Abi Talib, peace be upon him, and it is a well-known view of Ibn Abbas. Those who held this view argued with several points:

First: His words ﴿the day when the sky brings smoke﴾ require that there be a smoke which the sky brings. What you have mentioned, the darkness occurring in the eye because of the severity of hunger, is not a smoke brought by the sky. Therefore, reading the verse in this way is a departure from its apparent meaning without a separate proof, and that is not permissible.

Second: He described that smoke as "clear" (mubin), and the condition you mentioned is not like that, because it is an incidental state that befalls some people in their brains, and such a thing cannot be described as a clear smoke.

Third: He described that smoke as "covering the people," and this is only true if the smoke reaches them and envelops them. The condition you mentioned can only be described as "covering the people" in a figurative sense, and we have already mentioned that a departure from the literal to the figurative is not permissible without a separate proof.

Fourth: It is related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "The first of the signs is the smoke, the descent of Jesus son of Mary, peace be upon them both, and a fire that will come out from the depths of Aden, driving people to the place of gathering." Hudhayfa said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is the smoke?" So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited the verse, and said: "A smoke that fills what is between the east and the west, remaining forty days and nights. As for the believer, it affects him like a cold in the head; as for the disbeliever, he is like a drunkard, coming out from his nostrils, ears and rear." This was narrated by the author of al-Kashshaf.

Al-Qadi related from al-Hasan, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "Hasten to good deeds before six things," and he mentioned among them the rising of the sun from its west, the Dajjal, the smoke, and the beast. As for those who hold the first opinion, there is no doubt that it requires diverting the word from its literal meaning to the figurative, and that is not permissible except when there is a proof showing that taking it in its literal sense is impossible. These people did not mention such a proof, so their position is very problematic. If they say: The proof that what we have mentioned is intended is that He, the Exalted, related of them that they say: ﴿Our Lord, remove the punishment from us; indeed we are believers﴾, and if we take this as the famine that occurred in Mecca, it is sound, for it is reported that when the famine in Mecca became severe, Abu Sufyan came to him, pleaded with him by Allah and by kinship, and promised that if he prayed for them and Allah removed that calamity from them, they would believe in him. When Allah, the Exalted, removed it from them, they returned to their polytheism. But if we take it to mean the appearance of one of the signs of the Resurrection, this would not be valid, because at the appearance of the signs of the Resurrection they cannot say: ﴿Our Lord, remove the punishment from us; indeed we are believers﴾, and it would also not be valid to say to them: ﴿Indeed We will remove the punishment a little, but you will surely return﴾. The answer is: Why could it not be that the appearance of this sign operates like the appearance of the other signs of the Resurrection, in that it does not cause the cessation of obligation, so this condition occurs; then people fear greatly and humble themselves, and when that affliction passes they return to disbelief and wickedness? If this is possible, then what they said falls away. And Allah knows best.

Let us return to the exegesis and say: His words, the Exalted, ﴿the day when the sky brings a clear smoke﴾ mean: in its apparent state, no one doubts that it is a smoke ﴿covering the people﴾, that is, encompassing them. The phrase ﴿covering the people﴾ is in the genitive position as an adjective of His words ﴿with smoke﴾. As for His words ﴿This is a painful punishment﴾, there are two opinions:

The first: It is in the accusative position by an implied verb, which is "they say," and "they say" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state, meaning: saying this.

The second: Al-Jurjani, the author of al-Nazm, said: "This" is a pointing to it and an announcement of its nearness and approach, as one says: "This enemy, so face him." The purpose of it is to draw attention to its closeness.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Our Lord, remove the punishment from us﴾. If we say the implied sentence is: "They say, 'This is a painful punishment. Our Lord, remove the punishment from us,'" the meaning is clear; and even if the saying is not implied there, we imply it here. The punishment, according to the first opinion, is the severe famine, and according to the second, it is the destruction. ﴿Indeed we are believers﴾, that is, in Muhammad and in the Qur'an; and what is meant is a promise of belief if the punishment is removed from them.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿How will they have the reminder﴾, meaning: How will they be reminded, and how will they be admonished by this condition, when there has come to them what is greater and more compelling in the obligation of obedience, namely what appeared upon the Messenger of Allah of overpowering miracles and dazzling clear signs? ﴿Then they turned away from him﴾ and did not pay attention to him, ﴿and said, "A taught one, a madman."﴾ This was because the disbelievers of Mecca had two views regarding the emergence of the Qur'an upon Muhammad, peace be upon him. Some of them used to say: Muhammad learns these words from some people, because of His words: ﴿The speech of the one they point to is foreign, while this is clear Arabic﴾ [al-Nahl: 103], and His words: ﴿Others helped him with it﴾ [al-Furqan: 4]. Others used to say: He is a madman, and the jinn cast these words upon him while he is in a state of fainting.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed We will remove the punishment a little, but you will surely return﴾, meaning: just as the punishment is removed from you, you will immediately return to what you were upon of polytheism. The purpose is to draw attention to the fact that they do not keep their promises, and that in a state of helplessness they humble themselves before Allah, the Exalted; but when the fear passes, they return to disbelief and to blind imitation of the ways of their ancestors.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿on the day We seize with the greatest seizing; indeed We will take vengeance.﴾ The author of al-Kashshaf said: It has been read as "nabtush" with a damma on the ta', and al-Hasan read "nubtish" with a damma on the nun, as if the Exalted were commanding the angels to seize them. "Al-batsh" means taking with force, and it most often occurs through a succession of striking blows; then it came to be used for inflicting successive pains. Regarding what is meant by this day, there are two opinions:

The first opinion: It is the Day of Badr. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Muqatil and Abu al-Aliya, may Allah the Exalted be pleased with them. They said: When Allah the Exalted removed from them the famine and hunger, they returned to denial, and so Allah took vengeance upon them on the Day of Badr.

The second opinion: It is the Day of Resurrection. Ikrima related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah the Exalted be pleased with them both, that he said: Ibn Mas'ud said: "The greatest seizing is the Day of Badr," and I say: It is the Day of Resurrection. This view is more correct, because the Day of Badr does not reach this level that would merit this great description; and because complete vengeance only takes place on the Day of Resurrection, according to His words, the Exalted: ﴿Today every soul will be recompensed for what it earned﴾ [Ghafir: 17]; and because, since this seizing has been described as "the greatest" without qualification, it must be the greatest kind of seizing, and that is none other than on the Resurrection. The word "vengeance" (intiqam) with respect to Allah, the Exalted, is among the ambiguous attributes, like anger, shyness and wonder; the meaning is known, and Allah knows best.

* * *

Some of them used to say: Muhammad learns these words from some people, because of His words: ﴿The speech of the one they point to is foreign, while this is clear Arabic﴾ [al-Nahl: 103], and His words: ﴿Others helped him with it﴾ [al-Furqan: 4]. Others used to say: He is a madman, and the jinn cast these words upon him while he is in a state of fainting.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed We will remove the punishment a little, but you will surely return﴾, meaning: just as the punishment is removed from you, you will immediately return to what you were upon of polytheism. The purpose is to draw attention to the fact that they do not keep their promises, and that in a state of helplessness they humble themselves before Allah, the Exalted; but when the fear passes, they return to disbelief and to blind imitation of the ways of their ancestors.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿on the day We seize with the greatest seizing; indeed We will take vengeance.﴾ The author of al-Kashshaf said: It has been read as "nabtush" with a damma on the ta', and al-Hasan read "nubtish" with a damma on the nun, as if the Exalted were commanding the angels to seize them. "Al-batsh" means taking with force, and it most often occurs through a succession of striking blows; then it came to be used for inflicting successive pains. Regarding what is meant by this day, there are two opinions:

The first opinion: It is the Day of Badr. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Muqatil and Abu al-Aliya, may Allah the Exalted be pleased with them. They said: When Allah the Exalted removed from them the famine and hunger, they returned to denial, and so Allah took vengeance upon them on the Day of Badr.

The second opinion: It is the Day of Resurrection. Ikrima related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah the Exalted be pleased with them both, that he said: Ibn Mas'ud said: "The greatest seizing is the Day of Badr," and I say: It is the Day of Resurrection. This view is more correct, because the Day of Badr does not reach this level that would merit this great description; and because complete vengeance only takes place on the Day of Resurrection, according to His words, the Exalted: ﴿Today every soul will be recompensed for what it earned﴾ [Ghafir: 17]; and because, since this seizing has been described as "the greatest" without qualification, it must be the greatest kind of seizing, and that is none other than on the Resurrection. The word "vengeance" (intiqam) with respect to Allah, the Exalted, is among the ambiguous attributes, like anger, shyness and wonder; the meaning is known, and Allah knows best.

صفحة ٢١٠
Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 44, verses 17–29:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We had already tested before them the people of Pharaoh, and there came to them a noble messenger﴾ ﴿Saying: "Deliver to me the servants of Allah. Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger"﴾ ﴿And do not exalt yourselves over Allah. Indeed, I bring you a clear authority﴾ ﴿And indeed, I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord, lest you stone me﴾ ﴿And if you do not believe me, then leave me alone﴾ ﴿So he called upon his Lord, "These are a criminal people"﴾ ﴿"So travel with My servants by night; indeed, you will be pursued"﴾ ﴿"And leave the sea parted. Indeed, they are an army to be drowned"﴾ ﴿How many they left behind of gardens and springs﴾ ﴿and crops and a noble station﴾ ﴿and luxury in which they had been pleasure-seeking﴾ ﴿Thus. And We bequeathed them to another people﴾ ﴿And the heaven and the earth did not weep for them, nor were they reprieved﴾.

صفحة ٢١٠
Know that when Allah, exalted is He, made clear that the disbelievers of Makkah persist in their disbelief, He made clear that many of the earlier peoples were likewise. So He showed the presence of this attribute in most of the people of Pharaoh. The author of al-Kashshaf said: it has been recited as (وَلَقَدْ فَتَّنَّا) with the shaddah for emphasis. Ibn Abbas said: "We tested." al-Zajjaj said: "We tried." The meaning is: We dealt with them as one who tests, by sending the messenger to them. ﴿And there came to them a noble messenger﴾, who was Musa. The commentators differed about the meaning of "noble" (karim) here. al-Kalbi said: "Noble before his Lord," meaning that he deserved from his Lord many kinds of honour. Muqatil said: "Good in character." al-Farra said: one says "So-and-so is the noble of his people," because a messenger was rarely sent except from among the nobles and the honourable of his people.
* * *
Then He said: ﴿Deliver to me the servants of Allah﴾. Regarding (أَنْ) there are two views:
The first: it is the explanatory (أَنِ المُفَسِّرَةُ, an-al-mufassirah, "that" introducing an explanation), because the coming of a messenger to those to whom he is sent implies the sense of speech, since he comes to them only as a bringer of good news, a warner, and one calling to Allah.

The second: it is the light form of the heavy (أَنَّ), and its meaning is: "And there came to them, that the matter and the word is: Deliver." "The servants of Allah" is the object, and they are the Children of Israel. He says: "Deliver them to me and send them with me." This is like His saying: ﴿So send with us the Children of Israel and do not torment them﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:47]. It is also permissible that it be a call to them, and the sense is: "Deliver to me, O servants of Allah, what is obligatory upon you of faith, acceptance of my call, and following my way." He gave as the reason for this that he is ﴿a trustworthy messenger﴾ whom Allah has entrusted with His revelation and His message.

﴿And do not exalt yourselves﴾: this (أَنْ) is like the first in both its possibilities, meaning: do not be arrogant toward Allah by insulting His revelation and His messenger. ﴿Indeed, I bring you a clear authority﴾: a manifest proof whose soundness every sensible person would acknowledge. ﴿And indeed, I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord, lest you stone me﴾: it has been said that the meaning is that you kill me; and it has been said that (lest you stone me) means with words, so that you say: "Sorcerer, liar." ﴿And if you do not believe me﴾, that is, if you do not confirm me and do not believe in Allah on account of the proof I have brought you, then the lam in (لِي) is the lam of cause (لَامُ الأَجَلِ). ﴿Then leave me alone﴾, that is, clear the way for me, neither for me nor against me.

The author of al-Kuttab (i.e., the author of this book), may Allah have mercy on him, said: The Mu'tazilah (a theological school) boast and say that the word "i'tizal" (withdrawal, separation) wherever it occurs in the Qur'an means withdrawal from falsehood, not from truth. It so happened that I was present at some gatherings, and one of them mentioned this statement, so I brought this verse against him and said: The meaning of "i'tizal" in this verse is withdrawal from the religion of Musa, peace be upon him, and his path, and that is without doubt withdrawal from the truth. So the man was silenced.

* * *
Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So he called upon his Lord﴾. The fa' in (فَدَعَا) indicates that it is connected to an omitted element before it. The interpretation is: They disbelieved and did not believe, so Musa called upon his Lord, "that these are a criminal people." If they say: Disbelief is graver in state than criminality, so what is the reason that the attribute of the disbelievers was made to be "criminals" at the time he intended to emphasise their blame? I say: because the disbeliever may be just in his religion, may be criminal in his religion, and may be a sinful person in his religion, the most vile of people. The author of al-Kashshaf said: it has been recited as (إِنَّ هَؤُلَاءِ) with the kasrah, on the assumption of an implied verb of saying, meaning: so he called upon his Lord and said: (Indeed these are a criminal people).
* * *
Then He said: ﴿So travel with My servants by night﴾. Ibn Kathir and Nafi' read (فَاسْرِ) with a connected alif, and the rest with a cut alif (فَأَسْرِ). (سَرَى) and (أَسْرَى) are two dialects, meaning: We revealed to Musa that he should travel with My servants by night, ﴿indeed you will be pursued﴾, that is, Pharaoh and his people will pursue you, and that will be a cause for their destruction.
صفحة ٢١١
﴿And leave the sea parted (rahwan)﴾. Regarding (الرَّهْو) there are two views:
One of them: it is the still (السَّاكِن). It is said: "A life of rahw" when it is comfortable and at ease. And say: "Do that heedlessly, rahw," meaning calmly, without haste. When Musa, peace be upon him, had crossed the sea, he wished to strike it with his staff so that it would close as it had been. So Allah, exalted is He, commanded him to leave it still in its state, remaining as it was in its splitting of the water and the path remaining dry, until the Copts entered it; then when they were within it, Allah closed it over them.

The second: that rahw is a wide gap. The meaning is: "a path with rahw," that is, a path with a gap, meaning the way that Allah made appear between the sea. ﴿Indeed they are an army to be drowned﴾, meaning: leave the path as it was, so that they enter and drown. Allah informed him of this only so that he would remain free of heart from their evil and their harm.

* * *
Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿How many they left behind of gardens and springs﴾ ﴿and crops and a noble station﴾. This verse shows that He drowned them, and then after their drowning He said this statement, and Allah, exalted is He, made clear that they left these five things: the gardens, the springs, the crops, and the noble station. By "the noble station" is meant the gatherings and good dwellings they had. It has been said: the pulpits upon which they used to praise Pharaoh. ﴿And luxury in which they had been pleasure-seeking﴾. The scholars of language said: (نَعْمَة) with a fatha on the nun means the goodness and freshness of life, and (نِعْمَة) of Allah is His beneficence and gift. The author of al-Kashshaf said: (نَعْمَة) with the fatha is from enjoying comfort, and with the kasrah is from bestowing favour. It has been recited (فَاكِهِينَ) and (فَكِهِينَ). (كَذَلِكَ): the kaf is in the accusative, in the sense of "the like of that expulsion: We expelled them from it and bequeathed it"; or it is in the nominative position, on the assumption that the matter is ﴿thus﴾. ﴿And We bequeathed them to another people﴾ who had no part of them in kinship, religion, or allegiance, and they were the Children of Israel, who had been enslaved in their hands; so Allah destroyed them at their hands and bequeathed to them their kingdom and their dwellings.
* * *
Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the heaven and the earth did not weep for them﴾, and regarding this there are several views:
The first: al-Wahidi said in al-Basit: It is narrated from Anas ibn Malik that the Prophet ﷺ said: "There is not a servant but that he has in the heaven two doors: a door from which his provision descends, and a door into which his deeds ascend. When he dies, they both lose him and weep over him." And he recited this verse, and said: That is because they did not do righteous deeds on earth so that it would weep for them, and no good word or righteous deed ascended to heaven for it to weep for them. This is the view of most of the commentators.

The second view: the estimation is: "The people of the heaven and the people of the earth did not weep for them," so the mudaf (the governed noun) has been omitted, and the meaning is: the angels did not weep for them, nor did the believers; rather, they were pleased with their destruction.

The third view: the custom of people is to say, upon the death of a man of great stature: "The world has grown dark for him, the sun and the moon were eclipsed on his account, and the wind, the heaven and the earth wept," and they intend to exaggerate the magnitude of that calamity, not the literal lie itself. The author of al-Kashshaf related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "No believer dies in a foreign land in which his weepers are absent, but that the heaven and the earth weep over him."

Jarir said:
The sun is rising; it is not eclipsed,
it weeps for you, the stars of the night and the moon.
In it there is something resembling mockery of them, meaning that they used to magnify themselves, and used to believe of themselves that if they died the heaven and the earth would weep for them. But they were not at this level; rather they were below that, and this is mentioned only by way of derision.

صفحة ٢١٢
Then He said: ﴿And they were not reprieved﴾, that is, when the time of their destruction came, they were not granted respite to another time for repentance, amends, or making up for their shortcomings.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We had already tested before them the people of Pharaoh, and there came to them a noble messenger﴾ ﴿Saying: "Deliver to me the servants of Allah. Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger"﴾ ﴿And do not exalt yourselves over Allah. Indeed, I bring you a clear authority﴾ ﴿And indeed, I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord, lest you stone me﴾ ﴿And if you do not believe me, then leave me alone﴾ ﴿So he called upon his Lord, "These are a criminal people"﴾ ﴿"So travel with My servants by night; indeed, you will be pursued"﴾ ﴿"And leave the sea parted. Indeed, they are an army to be drowned"﴾ ﴿How many they left behind of gardens and springs﴾ ﴿and crops and a noble station﴾ ﴿and luxury in which they had been pleasure-seeking﴾ ﴿Thus. And We bequeathed them to another people﴾ ﴿And the heaven and the earth did not weep for them, nor were they reprieved﴾.

صفحة ٢١٠
Know that when Allah, exalted is He, made clear that the disbelievers of Makkah persist in their disbelief, He made clear that many of the earlier peoples were likewise. So He showed the presence of this attribute in most of the people of Pharaoh. The author of al-Kashshaf said: it has been recited as (وَلَقَدْ فَتَّنَّا) with the shaddah for emphasis. Ibn Abbas said: "We tested." al-Zajjaj said: "We tried." The meaning is: We dealt with them as one who tests, by sending the messenger to them. ﴿And there came to them a noble messenger﴾, who was Musa. The commentators differed about the meaning of "noble" (karim) here. al-Kalbi said: "Noble before his Lord," meaning that he deserved from his Lord many kinds of honour. Muqatil said: "Good in character." al-Farra said: one says "So-and-so is the noble of his people," because a messenger was rarely sent except from among the nobles and the honourable of his people.
* * *
Then He said: ﴿Deliver to me the servants of Allah﴾. Regarding (أَنْ) there are two views:
The first: it is the explanatory (أَنِ المُفَسِّرَةُ, an-al-mufassirah, "that" introducing an explanation), because the coming of a messenger to those to whom he is sent implies the sense of speech, since he comes to them only as a bringer of good news, a warner, and one calling to Allah.

The second: it is the light form of the heavy (أَنَّ), and its meaning is: "And there came to them, that the matter and the word is: Deliver." "The servants of Allah" is the object, and they are the Children of Israel. He says: "Deliver them to me and send them with me." This is like His saying: ﴿So send with us the Children of Israel and do not torment them﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:47]. It is also permissible that it be a call to them, and the sense is: "Deliver to me, O servants of Allah, what is obligatory upon you of faith, acceptance of my call, and following my way." He gave as the reason for this that he is ﴿a trustworthy messenger﴾ whom Allah has entrusted with His revelation and His message.

﴿And do not exalt yourselves﴾: this (أَنْ) is like the first in both its possibilities, meaning: do not be arrogant toward Allah by insulting His revelation and His messenger. ﴿Indeed, I bring you a clear authority﴾: a manifest proof whose soundness every sensible person would acknowledge. ﴿And indeed, I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord, lest you stone me﴾: it has been said that the meaning is that you kill me; and it has been said that (lest you stone me) means with words, so that you say: "Sorcerer, liar." ﴿And if you do not believe me﴾, that is, if you do not confirm me and do not believe in Allah on account of the proof I have brought you, then the lam in (لِي) is the lam of cause (لَامُ الأَجَلِ). ﴿Then leave me alone﴾, that is, clear the way for me, neither for me nor against me.

The author of al-Kuttab (i.e., the author of this book), may Allah have mercy on him, said: The Mu'tazilah (a theological school) boast and say that the word "i'tizal" (withdrawal, separation) wherever it occurs in the Qur'an means withdrawal from falsehood, not from truth. It so happened that I was present at some gatherings, and one of them mentioned this statement, so I brought this verse against him and said: The meaning of "i'tizal" in this verse is withdrawal from the religion of Musa, peace be upon him, and his path, and that is without doubt withdrawal from the truth. So the man was silenced.

* * *
Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So he called upon his Lord﴾. The fa' in (فَدَعَا) indicates that it is connected to an omitted element before it. The interpretation is: They disbelieved and did not believe, so Musa called upon his Lord, "that these are a criminal people." If they say: Disbelief is graver in state than criminality, so what is the reason that the attribute of the disbelievers was made to be "criminals" at the time he intended to emphasise their blame? I say: because the disbeliever may be just in his religion, may be criminal in his religion, and may be a sinful person in his religion, the most vile of people. The author of al-Kashshaf said: it has been recited as (إِنَّ هَؤُلَاءِ) with the kasrah, on the assumption of an implied verb of saying, meaning: so he called upon his Lord and said: (Indeed these are a criminal people).
* * *
Then He said: ﴿So travel with My servants by night﴾. Ibn Kathir and Nafi' read (فَاسْرِ) with a connected alif, and the rest with a cut alif (فَأَسْرِ). (سَرَى) and (أَسْرَى) are two dialects, meaning: We revealed to Musa that he should travel with My servants by night, ﴿indeed you will be pursued﴾, that is, Pharaoh and his people will pursue you, and that will be a cause for their destruction.
صفحة ٢١١
﴿And leave the sea parted (rahwan)﴾. Regarding (الرَّهْو) there are two views:
One of them: it is the still (السَّاكِن). It is said: "A life of rahw" when it is comfortable and at ease. And say: "Do that heedlessly, rahw," meaning calmly, without haste. When Musa, peace be upon him, had crossed the sea, he wished to strike it with his staff so that it would close as it had been. So Allah, exalted is He, commanded him to leave it still in its state, remaining as it was in its splitting of the water and the path remaining dry, until the Copts entered it; then when they were within it, Allah closed it over them.

The second: that rahw is a wide gap. The meaning is: "a path with rahw," that is, a path with a gap, meaning the way that Allah made appear between the sea. ﴿Indeed they are an army to be drowned﴾, meaning: leave the path as it was, so that they enter and drown. Allah informed him of this only so that he would remain free of heart from their evil and their harm.

* * *
Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿How many they left behind of gardens and springs﴾ ﴿and crops and a noble station﴾. This verse shows that He drowned them, and then after their drowning He said this statement, and Allah, exalted is He, made clear that they left these five things: the gardens, the springs, the crops, and the noble station. By "the noble station" is meant the gatherings and good dwellings they had. It has been said: the pulpits upon which they used to praise Pharaoh. ﴿And luxury in which they had been pleasure-seeking﴾. The scholars of language said: (نَعْمَة) with a fatha on the nun means the goodness and freshness of life, and (نِعْمَة) of Allah is His beneficence and gift. The author of al-Kashshaf said: (نَعْمَة) with the fatha is from enjoying comfort, and with the kasrah is from bestowing favour. It has been recited (فَاكِهِينَ) and (فَكِهِينَ). (كَذَلِكَ): the kaf is in the accusative, in the sense of "the like of that expulsion: We expelled them from it and bequeathed it"; or it is in the nominative position, on the assumption that the matter is ﴿thus﴾. ﴿And We bequeathed them to another people﴾ who had no part of them in kinship, religion, or allegiance, and they were the Children of Israel, who had been enslaved in their hands; so Allah destroyed them at their hands and bequeathed to them their kingdom and their dwellings.
* * *
Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the heaven and the earth did not weep for them﴾, and regarding this there are several views:
The first: al-Wahidi said in al-Basit: It is narrated from Anas ibn Malik that the Prophet ﷺ said: "There is not a servant but that he has in the heaven two doors: a door from which his provision descends, and a door into which his deeds ascend. When he dies, they both lose him and weep over him." And he recited this verse, and said: That is because they did not do righteous deeds on earth so that it would weep for them, and no good word or righteous deed ascended to heaven for it to weep for them. This is the view of most of the commentators.

The second view: the estimation is: "The people of the heaven and the people of the earth did not weep for them," so the mudaf (the governed noun) has been omitted, and the meaning is: the angels did not weep for them, nor did the believers; rather, they were pleased with their destruction.

The third view: the custom of people is to say, upon the death of a man of great stature: "The world has grown dark for him, the sun and the moon were eclipsed on his account, and the wind, the heaven and the earth wept," and they intend to exaggerate the magnitude of that calamity, not the literal lie itself. The author of al-Kashshaf related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "No believer dies in a foreign land in which his weepers are absent, but that the heaven and the earth weep over him."

Jarir said:
The sun is rising; it is not eclipsed,
it weeps for you, the stars of the night and the moon.
In it there is something resembling mockery of them, meaning that they used to magnify themselves, and used to believe of themselves that if they died the heaven and the earth would weep for them. But they were not at this level; rather they were below that, and this is mentioned only by way of derision.

صفحة ٢١٢
Then He said: ﴿And they were not reprieved﴾, that is, when the time of their destruction came, they were not granted respite to another time for repentance, amends, or making up for their shortcomings.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We certainly delivered the Children of Israel from the humiliating torment,﴾ ﴿from Pharaoh. Indeed, he was haughty and among the extravagant.﴾ ﴿And We certainly chose them knowingly over the worlds,﴾ ﴿and We gave them of the signs that contained a manifest trial.﴾ ﴿Indeed, these [people] are saying,﴾ ﴿"It is not but our first death, and we will not be resurrected.﴾ ﴿So bring our forefathers, if you are truthful."﴾ ﴿Are they better, or the people of Tubba' (a title of the kings of Yemen) and those before them? We destroyed them, for they were criminals.﴾ ﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play.﴾ ﴿We did not create them except with truth, but most of them do not know.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, explained how Pharaoh and his people were destroyed, He explained how He bestowed favour upon Musa and his people. Know that averting harm takes precedence over bringing benefit. So He, exalted is He, began by explaining the averting of harm from them, and said: ﴿And We certainly delivered the Children of Israel from the humiliating torment,﴾ meaning the killing of their sons, the keeping of their women alive for service, and the exhausting of them in arduous labour.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿from Pharaoh﴾, and in this there are two views:

The first: the meaning is "from the humiliating torment that proceeded from Pharaoh."

The second: Pharaoh is in apposition to "the humiliating torment," as if he himself was a humiliating torment, because of his excess in torturing and humiliating them.

The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: it has also been read as "min 'adhabi al-muhin" (from the torment of the one who humiliates), and according to this reading, "al-muhin" is Pharaoh, because he was greatly zealous in humiliating the righteous. In the reading of Ibn 'Abbas it is "man Fir'awnu" (who is Pharaoh), which is in the sense of a question, and His saying: ﴿Indeed, he was haughty and among the extravagant﴾ is its answer, as if the implied meaning is: "Do you know who he is in his tyranny and rebellion?" Then He described his condition by His saying: ﴿Indeed, he was haughty and among the extravagant﴾, that is, he was high in rank among the extravagant. It is also permissible that the meaning be ﴿Indeed, he was haughty﴾ in accordance with His saying: ﴿Indeed, Pharaoh exalted himself in the land﴾ [al-Qasas: 4], and he was also extravagant. Among his extravagance was that, despite his lowliness and baseness, he claimed divinity. When Allah, exalted is He, explained how He averted harm from the Children of Israel, He explained how He brought good things to them, and said: ﴿And We certainly chose them knowingly over the worlds﴾. In this there are two discussions:

The first discussion: His saying ﴿knowingly﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). Then there are two views in it:

One of them: that is, knowing that they deserved to be chosen and preferred over others.

The second: the meaning is "with Our knowledge that they may deviate and that lapses may proceed from them in some circumstances."

The second discussion: the apparent meaning of His saying ﴿And We certainly chose them knowingly over the worlds﴾ requires that they were better than all the worlds. It has been said: the meaning is "over the worlds of their time." It has also been said: this is a general statement into which specification has entered, like His saying: ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind﴾ [Al 'Imran: 110].

* * *

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We gave them of the signs﴾, such as the splitting of the sea, the shading by the cloud, the sending down of manna and quails, and others of the overpowering signs which Allah did not manifest the like of to anyone other than them, ﴿that contained a manifest trial﴾, that is, a manifest blessing. Because He, exalted is He, tests with affliction, He may also test with blessing, as a clear trial, so that the sincere (siddiq) may be distinguished from the heretic (zindiq). Here ends the discussion of the story of Musa, peace be upon him, and then He returned to mention the disbelievers of Makkah. This is because the discussion concerned them when He said: ﴿Rather, they are in doubt, playing﴾, that is, rather, they are in doubt about the resurrection and the Last Day. Then He explained the manner of their persistence in their disbelief, then He explained that the people of Pharaoh were persistent in disbelief in this same manner, then He explained how He destroyed them and how He bestowed favour upon the Children of Israel. Then He returned to the first topic, which is that the disbelievers of Makkah denied the resurrection, and said: ﴿Indeed, these [people] are saying, "It is not but our first death, and we will not be resurrected."﴾ If it is asked: the people were denying the second life, so was it not proper for them to say: "It is not but our first life, and we will not be resurrected"? We say: it was said to them: "Indeed, you will die a death that will be followed by a life, just as you, while you were sperm-drops, were dead, and that too will be followed by a life." That is His saying: ﴿And you were dead and He gave you life; then He will cause you to die; then He will bring you to life again﴾ [al-Baqarah: 28]. So they said: ﴿It is not but our first death﴾, meaning: what death is it that by its nature is followed by life, other than the first death, not the second death? And this attribute you ascribe to death, namely that life follows it, belongs to the first death alone. There is therefore no difference between this statement and His saying: ﴿It is not but our life of this world﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 37]. This is what the author of al-Kashshaf mentioned. It is possible to mention another view in this, and it is said: His saying ﴿It is not but our first death﴾ means: nothing comes to us of states except the first death. This statement indicates that the second life never comes to them at all. Then they stated this implied meaning explicitly, saying: ﴿and we will not be resurrected﴾. Thus there is no need for the artificial interpretation that the author of al-Kashshaf mentioned.

* * *

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿and we will not be resurrected﴾. It is said: Allah raised the dead (nashara) and resurrected them (anshara) when He brought them back to life. Then the disbelievers argued for the denial of gathering and resurrection by saying: "If resurrection and rising again are possible and rational, then make for us the revival of whoever of our forefathers has died, by asking your Lord for that, so that this becomes for us a proof of the truth of your claim regarding prophethood and the resurrection on the Day of Judgment." It was said: they asked the Messenger ﷺ to supplicate to Allah so that Qusayy ibn Kilab would be raised, so that they could consult him about the soundness of the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ and about the soundness of resurrection. When Allah related this from them, He said: ﴿Are they better, or the people of Tubba' and those before them? We destroyed them, for they were criminals.﴾ The meaning is that the disbelievers of Makkah did not mention in denying gathering and resurrection any doubt that would need an answer; rather, they persisted in ignorance and imitation in that denial. For this reason Allah, exalted is He, limited Himself to the threat, saying: the rest of the disbelievers were stronger than these, and Allah destroyed them, so likewise He will destroy these. So His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Are they better, or the people of Tubba'﴾ is a rhetorical question in the manner of denial. Abu 'Ubaydah said: the kings of Yemen, each one of them was called Tubba', because the people of the world followed him (yatba'unahu); and the status of Tubba' in the Jahiliyyah was like the status of the caliph in Islam, and they were the greatest of the kings of the Arabs. 'A'ishah said: Tubba' was a righteous man. Ka'b said: Allah censured his people but did not censure him. Al-Kalbi said: he is Abu Karib As'ad. And from the Prophet ﷺ: ("Do not revile Tubba', for he had embraced Islam. I do not know whether Tubba' was a prophet or not a prophet.") If it is asked: what is the meaning of His saying ﴿Are they better, or the people of Tubba'﴾, when there is no good in either group? We say: its meaning is: are they better in strength and might? Like His saying: ﴿Are your disbelievers better than those?﴾ [al-Qamar: 43], after mentioning the family of Pharaoh. Then He, exalted is He, mentioned the decisive proof for the doctrine of resurrection and the Last Day, saying: ﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play.﴾ Had there been no resurrection, this creation would have been play and futility. The establishment of this line of argument has been discussed in detail at the beginning of Surah Yunus, and at the end of Surah "Qad aflaha al-mu'minun," where He said: ﴿Did you think that We created you for no purpose?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 115], and in Surah Sad, where He said: ﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vanity﴾ [Sad: 27].

* * *

Then He said: ﴿We did not create them except with truth, but most of them do not know.﴾ The intended meaning is the people of Makkah. As for the Mu'tazilah's (the Mu'tazilites') use of this verse as evidence that He, exalted is He, does not create disbelief and immorality and does not will them, that is known together with its refutation. And Allah knows best.

In this there are two discussions:

The first discussion: His saying ﴿knowingly﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). Then there are two views in it:

One of them: that is, knowing that they deserved to be chosen and preferred over others.

The second: the meaning is "with Our knowledge that they may deviate and that lapses may proceed from them in some circumstances."

The second discussion: the apparent meaning of His saying ﴿And We certainly chose them knowingly over the worlds﴾ requires that they were better than all the worlds. Because He, exalted is He, tests with affliction, He may also test with blessing, as a clear trial, so that the sincere (siddiq) may be distinguished from the heretic (zindiq). Here ends the discussion of the story of Musa, peace be upon him, and then He returned to mention the disbelievers of Makkah. This is because the discussion concerned them when He said: ﴿Rather, they are in doubt, playing﴾, that is, rather, they are in doubt about the resurrection and the Last Day. Then He explained the manner of their persistence in their disbelief, then He explained that the people of Pharaoh were persistent in disbelief in this same manner, then He explained how He destroyed them and how He bestowed favour upon the Children of Israel. Then He returned to the first topic, which is that the disbelievers of Makkah denied the resurrection, and said: ﴿Indeed, these [people] are saying, "It is not but our first death, and we will not be resurrected."﴾ If it is asked: the people were denying the second life, so was it not proper for them to say: "It is not but our first life, and we will not be resurrected"? So they said: ﴿It is not but our first death﴾, meaning: what death is it that by its nature is followed by life, other than the first death, not the second death? There is therefore no difference between this statement and His saying: ﴿It is not but our life of this world﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 37]. This is what the author of al-Kashshaf mentioned. It is possible to mention another view in this, and it is said: His saying ﴿It is not but our first death﴾ means: nothing comes to us of states except the first death. Thus there is no need for the artificial interpretation that the author of al-Kashshaf mentioned.

* * *

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿and we will not be resurrected﴾. It is said: Allah raised the dead (nashara) and resurrected them (anshara) when He brought them back to life. Then the disbelievers argued for the denial of gathering and resurrection by saying: "If resurrection and rising again are possible and rational, then make for us the revival of whoever of our forefathers has died, by asking your Lord for that, so that this becomes for us a proof of the truth of your claim regarding prophethood and the resurrection on the Day of Judgment." It was said: they asked the Messenger ﷺ to supplicate to Allah so that Qusayy ibn Kilab would be raised, so that they could consult him about the soundness of the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ and about the soundness of resurrection. When Allah related this from them, He said: ﴿Are they better, or the people of Tubba' and those before them? We destroyed them, for they were criminals.﴾ The meaning is that the disbelievers of Makkah did not mention in denying gathering and resurrection any doubt that would need an answer; rather, they persisted in ignorance and imitation in that denial. And Allah knows best.
