The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: it has also been read as "min 'adhabi al-muhin" (from the torment of the one who humiliates), and according to this reading, "al-muhin" is Pharaoh, because he was greatly zealous in humiliating the righteous. In the reading of Ibn 'Abbas it is "man Fir'awnu" (who is Pharaoh), which is in the sense of a question, and His saying: ﴿Indeed, he was haughty and among the extravagant﴾ is its answer, as if the implied meaning is: "Do you know who he is in his tyranny and rebellion?" Then He described his condition by His saying: ﴿Indeed, he was haughty and among the extravagant﴾, that is, he was high in rank among the extravagant. It is also permissible that the meaning be ﴿Indeed, he was haughty﴾ in accordance with His saying: ﴿Indeed, Pharaoh exalted himself in the land﴾ [al-Qasas: 4], and he was also extravagant. Among his extravagance was that, despite his lowliness and baseness, he claimed divinity. When Allah, exalted is He, explained how He averted harm from the Children of Israel, He explained how He brought good things to them, and said: ﴿And We certainly chose them knowingly over the worlds﴾. In this there are two discussions:

The first discussion: His saying ﴿knowingly﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). Then there are two views in it:

One of them: that is, knowing that they deserved to be chosen and preferred over others.

The second: the meaning is "with Our knowledge that they may deviate and that lapses may proceed from them in some circumstances."

The second discussion: the apparent meaning of His saying ﴿And We certainly chose them knowingly over the worlds﴾ requires that they were better than all the worlds. It has been said: the meaning is "over the worlds of their time." It has also been said: this is a general statement into which specification has entered, like His saying: ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind﴾ [Al 'Imran: 110].

* * *

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We gave them of the signs﴾, such as the splitting of the sea, the shading by the cloud, the sending down of manna and quails, and others of the overpowering signs which Allah did not manifest the like of to anyone other than them, ﴿that contained a manifest trial﴾, that is, a manifest blessing. Because He, exalted is He, tests with affliction, He may also test with blessing, as a clear trial, so that the sincere (siddiq) may be distinguished from the heretic (zindiq). Here ends the discussion of the story of Musa, peace be upon him, and then He returned to mention the disbelievers of Makkah. This is because the discussion concerned them when He said: ﴿Rather, they are in doubt, playing﴾, that is, rather, they are in doubt about the resurrection and the Last Day. Then He explained the manner of their persistence in their disbelief, then He explained that the people of Pharaoh were persistent in disbelief in this same manner, then He explained how He destroyed them and how He bestowed favour upon the Children of Israel. Then He returned to the first topic, which is that the disbelievers of Makkah denied the resurrection, and said: ﴿Indeed, these [people] are saying, "It is not but our first death, and we will not be resurrected."﴾ If it is asked: the people were denying the second life, so was it not proper for them to say: "It is not but our first life, and we will not be resurrected"? We say: it was said to them: "Indeed, you will die a death that will be followed by a life, just as you, while you were sperm-drops, were dead, and that too will be followed by a life." That is His saying: ﴿And you were dead and He gave you life; then He will cause you to die; then He will bring you to life again﴾ [al-Baqarah: 28]. So they said: ﴿It is not but our first death﴾, meaning: what death is it that by its nature is followed by life, other than the first death, not the second death? And this attribute you ascribe to death, namely that life follows it, belongs to the first death alone. There is therefore no difference between this statement and His saying: ﴿It is not but our life of this world﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 37]. This is what the author of al-Kashshaf mentioned. It is possible to mention another view in this, and it is said: His saying ﴿It is not but our first death﴾ means: nothing comes to us of states except the first death. This statement indicates that the second life never comes to them at all. Then they stated this implied meaning explicitly, saying: ﴿and we will not be resurrected﴾. Thus there is no need for the artificial interpretation that the author of al-Kashshaf mentioned.

* * *

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿and we will not be resurrected﴾. It is said: Allah raised the dead (nashara) and resurrected them (anshara) when He brought them back to life. Then the disbelievers argued for the denial of gathering and resurrection by saying: "If resurrection and rising again are possible and rational, then make for us the revival of whoever of our forefathers has died, by asking your Lord for that, so that this becomes for us a proof of the truth of your claim regarding prophethood and the resurrection on the Day of Judgment." It was said: they asked the Messenger ﷺ to supplicate to Allah so that Qusayy ibn Kilab would be raised, so that they could consult him about the soundness of the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ and about the soundness of resurrection. When Allah related this from them, He said: ﴿Are they better, or the people of Tubba' and those before them? We destroyed them, for they were criminals.﴾ The meaning is that the disbelievers of Makkah did not mention in denying gathering and resurrection any doubt that would need an answer; rather, they persisted in ignorance and imitation in that denial. For this reason Allah, exalted is He, limited Himself to the threat, saying: the rest of the disbelievers were stronger than these, and Allah destroyed them, so likewise He will destroy these. So His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Are they better, or the people of Tubba'﴾ is a rhetorical question in the manner of denial. Abu 'Ubaydah said: the kings of Yemen, each one of them was called Tubba', because the people of the world followed him (yatba'unahu); and the status of Tubba' in the Jahiliyyah was like the status of the caliph in Islam, and they were the greatest of the kings of the Arabs. 'A'ishah said: Tubba' was a righteous man. Ka'b said: Allah censured his people but did not censure him. Al-Kalbi said: he is Abu Karib As'ad. And from the Prophet ﷺ: ("Do not revile Tubba', for he had embraced Islam. I do not know whether Tubba' was a prophet or not a prophet.") If it is asked: what is the meaning of His saying ﴿Are they better, or the people of Tubba'﴾, when there is no good in either group? We say: its meaning is: are they better in strength and might? Like His saying: ﴿Are your disbelievers better than those?﴾ [al-Qamar: 43], after mentioning the family of Pharaoh. Then He, exalted is He, mentioned the decisive proof for the doctrine of resurrection and the Last Day, saying: ﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play.﴾ Had there been no resurrection, this creation would have been play and futility. The establishment of this line of argument has been discussed in detail at the beginning of Surah Yunus, and at the end of Surah "Qad aflaha al-mu'minun," where He said: ﴿Did you think that We created you for no purpose?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 115], and in Surah Sad, where He said: ﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vanity﴾ [Sad: 27].

* * *

Then He said: ﴿We did not create them except with truth, but most of them do not know.﴾ The intended meaning is the people of Makkah. As for the Mu'tazilah's (the Mu'tazilites') use of this verse as evidence that He, exalted is He, does not create disbelief and immorality and does not will them, that is known together with its refutation. And Allah knows best.

[Page 213]

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 44, verse 40–50:

Allah, may He be exalted, says: ﴿Indeed, the Day of Decision is the appointed time for them all.﴾ ﴿The Day when no protector will avail a protégé at all, nor will they be helped.﴾ ﴿Except for those on whom Allah has mercy. Indeed, He is the Almighty, the Most Merciful.﴾ ﴿Indeed, the tree of al-Zaqqum﴾ ﴿is the food of the sinner.﴾ ﴿Like molten brass, it boils in the bellies,﴾ ﴿like the boiling of scalding water.﴾ ﴿Seize him and drag him into the midst of the Blazing Fire.﴾ ﴿Then pour over his head some of the torment of scalding water.﴾ ﴿Taste! Indeed, you were the mighty, the noble.﴾ ﴿Indeed, this is what you used to doubt.﴾

Know that the purpose of His saying: ﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play﴾ is to establish the saying of resurrection and the Last Day. Therefore, He mentioned immediately after it His saying: ﴿Indeed, the Day of Decision is the appointed time for them all﴾. And in naming the Day of Resurrection "the Day of Decision" there are several aspects:

The first: al-Hasan said: Allah separates therein between the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire.

The second: He makes a decision and judgment among His servants.

The third: For the believers it is the Day of Decision, in the sense that He separates them from everything they dislike; and for the disbelievers, in the sense that He separates them from everything they desire.

The fourth: The condition of each person becomes manifest as it truly is, so that no doubt or suspicion remains in their state; the illusions and doubts are separated, and the realities and clear proofs remain.

Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: The meaning is that on the day the Most Merciful separates His servants, their appointed time is for all of them, the pious and the wicked. Then He described that day, saying: ﴿The Day when no protector will avail a protégé at all﴾, meaning: a close relative will not avail a close relative. ﴿Nor will they be helped﴾, that is, they will have no helper. The meaning is that whoever might be expected to give help, whether a close relative in religion or in lineage or a freed slave, all of these are called "mawla" (protector); so when help does not come from them, it is even less likely to come from anyone else. This verse is similar to His saying: ﴿And fear a Day when no soul will avail another soul at all﴾ up to His saying: ﴿nor will they be helped﴾. Al-Wahidi said: What is meant by His saying: ﴿protégé from protector﴾ is the disbelievers. Do you not see that He mentioned the believer, saying: ﴿except for those on whom Allah has mercy﴾? Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: He means the believer, for the prophets and the angels will intercede for him.

Know that when He, may He be exalted, established the proof that the saying of the Resurrection is true, and then followed it with a description of that day, He mentioned immediately after it the threat for the disbelievers, and after it the promise for the righteous. As for the threat for the disbelievers, it is His saying: ﴿Indeed, the tree of al-Zaqqum, the food of the sinner﴾, and in it are several issues:

The first issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: It was read as "inna shijrata al-zaqqum" with a kasra on the shin. Then he said: There are three dialects in it: shajara with a fatha and with a kasra on the shin, shayara with a ya, and shabara with a ba.

The second issue: The discussion about the derivation of the word al-Zaqqum has already been presented in Surat al-Saffat, so there is no benefit in repeating it.

The third issue: The Mu'tazilah said: The verse indicates that this severe threat is realized for the sinner (al-atheem), and the sinner is one from whom sin has proceeded; so this threat would apply to the transgressors. The answer: We have explained in the principles of jurisprudence that a singular noun preceded by the definite article is originally understood to refer to what was previously mentioned, and does not indicate generality; and here the previously mentioned is the disbeliever, so it refers to him.

The fourth issue: The position of Abu Hanifa is that reciting the Qur'an by its meaning is permissible, and he argued for it by reporting that Ibn Mas'ud used to teach a man this verse and would say: "ṭaʿām al-laʾīm" (the food of the base one), and he said: Say: "ṭaʿām al-fājir" (the food of the wicked one). This evidence is extremely weak, as we have explained in the principles of jurisprudence.

Then he said: "Like molten brass" (kal-muhl) is read with a damma and with a fatha on the mim, and its explanation has preceded in Surat al-Kahf. Allah has likened this food to al-muhl, which is the dregs of oil, the sediment of tar, melted copper, and all other metals. The sentence is complete here; then He informed of its boiling in the bellies of the disbelievers, saying: ﴿it boils in the bellies﴾. It is read with a ta' and whoever reads with a ta' does so because the tree is feminine; and whoever reads with a ya' takes it to refer to the food in His saying: ﴿the food of the sinner﴾, because the food is, in meaning, the fruit of the tree. Abu ʿUbayd preferred the ya', because the noun mentioned, namely al-muhl, is the one immediately adjacent to the verb, so masculine agreement with it is preferable. Know that it is not permissible to attribute the boiling (ghalayan) to al-muhl, because al-muhl is the thing likened, and only that which is likened to al-muhl boils, such as the boiling of scalding water (al-hamim); and when the boiling of water becomes intense, it is hamim.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Seize him﴾, that is, seize the sinner. ﴿and drag him﴾ is read with a kasra on the ta'. Al-Layth said: al-ʿatl is that you take a man by the shoulder and drag him toward you, that is, pull him, and take him to a prison or a torment. And so-and-so took hold of the camel's halter, ya'tiluha, which is when he grips the base of the halter near the head and leads her with a violent pulling. Ibn al-Sikkit said: ʿatalahu to the prison and aʿtalahu when you push him with a violent push. This is the statement of all the lexicographers regarding ʿatl, and they mentioned for both dialects the damma and kasra on the ta', and both are sound, like yaʿkufuna and yaʿkifuna, and yaʿrushuna and yaʿrishuna.

His saying: ﴿into the midst of the Blazing Fire﴾, that is, into the middle of the Blazing Fire. ﴿Then pour over his head some of the torment of scalding water﴾. The original form would have been to say: "Then pour over him the scalding water from above his head," or "scalding water be poured from above their heads," but this metaphor is more complete in exaggeration, as if He is saying: pour upon him the torment of that scalding water. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿Our Lord, pour upon us patience﴾ [al-Baqarah: 250]. As for ﴿Taste! Indeed, you were the mighty, the noble﴾, they mentioned several aspects regarding it:

The first: that he is addressed with this in mockery, and the meaning is: you are the opposite of that.

The second: that Abu Jahl said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Between its two mountains there is no one mightier or more noble than me; by Allah, neither you nor your Lord can do anything to me."

The third: that you used to glory not in Allah; so look at what you have fallen into. It is also read as "annaka" with the sense of "because you."

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Indeed, this is what you used to doubt﴾, that is, this punishment is what you used to doubt, meaning you were skeptical about it. What is meant by it is what He mentioned at the beginning of the surah, where He said: ﴿Rather, they are in doubt, playing﴾.

Then He said: ﴿Indeed, this is what you used to doubt﴾, that is, this punishment is what you used to doubt, meaning you were skeptical about it. What is meant by it is what He mentioned at the beginning of the surah, where He said: ﴿Rather, they are in doubt, playing﴾.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 44, verse 40–50:

Allah, may He be exalted, says: ﴿Indeed, the Day of Decision is the appointed time for them all.﴾ ﴿The Day when no protector will avail a protégé at all, nor will they be helped.﴾ ﴿Except for those on whom Allah has mercy. Indeed, He is the Almighty, the Most Merciful.﴾ ﴿Indeed, the tree of al-Zaqqum﴾ ﴿is the food of the sinner.﴾ ﴿Like molten brass, it boils in the bellies,﴾ ﴿like the boiling of scalding water.﴾ ﴿Seize him and drag him into the midst of the Blazing Fire.﴾ ﴿Then pour over his head some of the torment of scalding water.﴾ ﴿Taste! Indeed, you were the mighty, the noble.﴾ ﴿Indeed, this is what you used to doubt.﴾

Know that the purpose of His saying: ﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play﴾ is to establish the saying of resurrection and the Last Day. Therefore, He mentioned immediately after it His saying: ﴿Indeed, the Day of Decision is the appointed time for them all﴾. And in naming the Day of Resurrection "the Day of Decision" there are several aspects:

The first: al-Hasan said: Allah separates therein between the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire.

The second: He makes a decision and judgment among His servants.

The third: For the believers it is the Day of Decision, in the sense that He separates them from everything they dislike; and for the disbelievers, in the sense that He separates them from everything they desire.

The fourth: The condition of each person becomes manifest as it truly is, so that no doubt or suspicion remains in their state; the illusions and doubts are separated, and the realities and clear proofs remain.

Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: The meaning is that on the day the Most Merciful separates His servants, their appointed time is for all of them, the pious and the wicked. Then He described that day, saying: ﴿The Day when no protector will avail a protégé at all﴾, meaning: a close relative will not avail a close relative. ﴿Nor will they be helped﴾, that is, they will have no helper. The meaning is that whoever might be expected to give help, whether a close relative in religion or in lineage or a freed slave, all of these are called "mawla" (protector); so when help does not come from them, it is even less likely to come from anyone else. This verse is similar to His saying: ﴿And fear a Day when no soul will avail another soul at all﴾ up to His saying: ﴿nor will they be helped﴾. Al-Wahidi said: What is meant by His saying: ﴿protégé from protector﴾ is the disbelievers. Do you not see that He mentioned the believer, saying: ﴿except for those on whom Allah has mercy﴾? Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: He means the believer, for the prophets and the angels will intercede for him.

Know that when He, may He be exalted, established the proof that the saying of the Resurrection is true, and then followed it with a description of that day, He mentioned immediately after it the threat for the disbelievers, and after it the promise for the righteous. As for the threat for the disbelievers, it is His saying: ﴿Indeed, the tree of al-Zaqqum, the food of the sinner﴾, and in it are several issues:

The first issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: It was read as "inna shijrata al-zaqqum" with a kasra on the shin. Then he said: There are three dialects in it: shajara with a fatha and with a kasra on the shin, shayara with a ya, and shabara with a ba.

The second issue: The discussion about the derivation of the word al-Zaqqum has already been presented in Surat al-Saffat, so there is no benefit in repeating it.

The third issue: The Mu'tazilah said: The verse indicates that this severe threat is realized for the sinner (al-atheem), and the sinner is one from whom sin has proceeded; so this threat would apply to the transgressors. The answer: We have explained in the principles of jurisprudence that a singular noun preceded by the definite article is originally understood to refer to what was previously mentioned, and does not indicate generality; and here the previously mentioned is the disbeliever, so it refers to him.

The fourth issue: The position of Abu Hanifa is that reciting the Qur'an by its meaning is permissible, and he argued for it by reporting that Ibn Mas'ud used to teach a man this verse and would say: "ṭaʿām al-laʾīm" (the food of the base one), and he said: Say: "ṭaʿām al-fājir" (the food of the wicked one). This evidence is extremely weak, as we have explained in the principles of jurisprudence.

Then he said: "Like molten brass" (kal-muhl) is read with a damma and with a fatha on the mim, and its explanation has preceded in Surat al-Kahf. Allah has likened this food to al-muhl, which is the dregs of oil, the sediment of tar, melted copper, and all other metals. The sentence is complete here; then He informed of its boiling in the bellies of the disbelievers, saying: ﴿it boils in the bellies﴾. It is read with a ta' and whoever reads with a ta' does so because the tree is feminine; and whoever reads with a ya' takes it to refer to the food in His saying: ﴿the food of the sinner﴾, because the food is, in meaning, the fruit of the tree. Abu ʿUbayd preferred the ya', because the noun mentioned, namely al-muhl, is the one immediately adjacent to the verb, so masculine agreement with it is preferable. Know that it is not permissible to attribute the boiling (ghalayan) to al-muhl, because al-muhl is the thing likened, and only that which is likened to al-muhl boils, such as the boiling of scalding water (al-hamim); and when the boiling of water becomes intense, it is hamim.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Seize him﴾, that is, seize the sinner. ﴿and drag him﴾ is read with a kasra on the ta'. Al-Layth said: al-ʿatl is that you take a man by the shoulder and drag him toward you, that is, pull him, and take him to a prison or a torment. And so-and-so took hold of the camel's halter, ya'tiluha, which is when he grips the base of the halter near the head and leads her with a violent pulling. Ibn al-Sikkit said: ʿatalahu to the prison and aʿtalahu when you push him with a violent push. This is the statement of all the lexicographers regarding ʿatl, and they mentioned for both dialects the damma and kasra on the ta', and both are sound, like yaʿkufuna and yaʿkifuna, and yaʿrushuna and yaʿrishuna.

His saying: ﴿into the midst of the Blazing Fire﴾, that is, into the middle of the Blazing Fire. ﴿Then pour over his head some of the torment of scalding water﴾. The original form would have been to say: "Then pour over him the scalding water from above his head," or "scalding water be poured from above their heads," but this metaphor is more complete in exaggeration, as if He is saying: pour upon him the torment of that scalding water. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿Our Lord, pour upon us patience﴾ [al-Baqarah: 250]. As for ﴿Taste! Indeed, you were the mighty, the noble﴾, they mentioned several aspects regarding it:

The first: that he is addressed with this in mockery, and the meaning is: you are the opposite of that.

The second: that Abu Jahl said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Between its two mountains there is no one mightier or more noble than me; by Allah, neither you nor your Lord can do anything to me."

The third: that you used to glory not in Allah; so look at what you have fallen into. It is also read as "annaka" with the sense of "because you."

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Indeed, this is what you used to doubt﴾, that is, this punishment is what you used to doubt, meaning you were skeptical about it. What is meant by it is what He mentioned at the beginning of the surah, where He said: ﴿Rather, they are in doubt, playing﴾.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 44, verse 51–59:

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be in a secure place, among gardens and springs, wearing silk and brocade, facing one another. So it will be, and We will pair them with houris, wide-eyed. There they will call for every kind of fruit, in security. They will not taste death therein, except the first death; and He will protect them from the punishment of the Blazing Fire, as a bounty from your Lord. That is the supreme triumph.  So We have made it easy in your tongue, that they may be reminded. So wait, for they are waiting.﴾

Know that when Allah the Exalted mentioned the threat in the preceding verses, He mentioned the promise in these verses, saying: ﴿Indeed, the God-fearing﴾. Our companions (the Ash'ari scholars) said: whoever guards against shirk has truly earned the name "muttaqi" (one who fears God), so the sinner (fasiq) must also be included in this promise.

Know that Allah the Exalted mentioned four of the causes of their comfort. The first of them is their dwellings, so He said: ﴿in a secure place﴾.

Know that a dwelling is only pleasant under two conditions:

The first: that it is safe from everything one fears and dreads, and this is what is meant by His words: ﴿in a secure place﴾. The majority of reciters read ﴿maqam﴾ with a fatha on the mim, while Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read it with a damma on the mim. The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: "Maqam" with a fatha is the place of standing, and what is meant is the place, which is one of the specific terms that has been used in the general sense. With a damma, it is the place of residing. "Amin" comes from your saying: "amina al-rajul amanatan, fa-huwa amin," and it is the opposite of "kha'in" (treacherous). It is attributed to the place metaphorically, because a frightening place seems to betray its occupant.

The second condition for the pleasantness of a place is that it contains the means of enjoyment, which are gardens and springs. When Allah the Exalted mentioned these two conditions regarding the dwellings of the people of Paradise, He described them with something that admits of no increase.

The second category of their comforts is clothing, so He said: ﴿They will wear silk and brocade﴾. It was said: "sundus" is the finer part of silk brocade, and "istabraq" is the thicker part of it, and it is an arabicized form of "istabrak." If they ask: how is a non-Arabic word found in the Qur'an? We say: once it has been arabicized, it has become Arabic.

Page 217
The third category is their sitting in a posture of facing one another, and the purpose of it is the companionship of some with others. If they say: sitting in this manner is unsettling, since each one of them would be aware of what the other does; and also, the one whose reward is less, when he sees the one whose reward is greater, his life would be embittered. We say: the conditions of the Hereafter are different from the conditions of this world.

The fourth category is their spouses. He said: ﴿So it will be, and We will pair them with houris﴾. The particle "ka" here has two possibilities: it may be in the nominative case, with the meaning "the matter is so," or in the accusative case, with the meaning "We gave them the like of that." Abu 'Ubayda said: "We made them spouses just as a husband is paired with a husband," that is, We made them two by two. They differed over whether this word indicates the occurrence of the marriage contract or not. Yunus said: His words ﴿and We paired them with houris﴾ mean "We joined them with them," so it is not a marriage contract, and the Arabs do not say "tazawwajtu bi-ha" (I married with her), but rather "tazawwajtuha" (I married her). Al-Wahidi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The revelation supports what Yunus said, and that is His words: ﴿Then when Zayd had accomplished his need from her, We gave her to you in marriage﴾ [al-Ahzab: 37]. Had the meaning been "tazawwajta bi-ha," it would have been "zawwajnaka biha." Moreover, the saying of the speaker "zawwajtuhu bihi" means that he was single, so I paired him with another, just as one says "shaffa'tuhu bi-akhar" (I made him a pair with another).

As for "hur," al-Wahidi said: the root of "hawar" is whiteness, and "tahwir" is whitening. We have mentioned this in the explanation of "al-hawariyyun." An eye is "hawra'" when the whiteness of its white becomes intense and the blackness of its black becomes intense, and a woman is not called "hawra'" until the whiteness of her eyes is whiteness in the color of her body. The evidence that "hawar" in this verse means white is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "bi-'isin 'in," and "al-'is" are white ones. As for "'in," it is the plural of "'ayna'," which is the woman with large, wide eyes. Al-Jubba'i said: a man is "a'yan" when his eye is large and wide, the feminine is "'ayna'," and the plural is "'in." Then they differed about these houris 'in: al-Hasan said: they are your old women with toothless gums, whom Allah will recreate as a different creation. Abu Hurayra said: they are not women of this world.

The fifth category of the comforts of the people of Paradise is food, so He said: ﴿There they will call for every kind of fruit, in security﴾. They said: they will eat all kinds of fruit, because they are safe from indigestion and diseases.

When Allah the Exalted described the kinds of good things and comforts they have, He made clear that their life is everlasting, so He said: ﴿They will not taste death therein, except the first death﴾. In this there are two questions:

The first question: they did not taste the first death in Paradise, so how is this exception appropriate? It has been answered in several ways:

The first: The author of al-Kashshaf said: the intention is to say, "They will not taste death at all," so His words ﴿except the first death﴾ were placed in the position of that, because a past death is impossible in the future, so it is of the type of suspension upon the impossible, as if it were said: If the first death were possible to taste in the future, then they would taste it.

The second: that "illa" (except) has the meaning of "lakinna" (but), and the meaning is: They will not taste death therein, but the first death they have already tasted.

The third: that the true reality of Paradise is the joy of the soul and its delight in knowing Allah the Exalted, obeying Him, and loving Him. When this is the case, the person who has attained this happiness is in Paradise in this world and also in the Hereafter. When this is so, the first death has occurred at the time when the person was in the true Paradise, which is the Paradise of knowledge of Allah and love. Thus, the mention of this exception is like an alert to our saying that the true Paradise is the attainment of this state, not the abode that is the place of eating and drinking. For this reason, he (peace be upon him) said: ("The prophets of Allah do not die, but they are transferred from one abode to another.")

The fourth: that whoever has experienced something and come to know it may correctly be said to have tasted it, and if it is correct to call knowledge by tasting, it is also correct to call remembering it by tasting. So His words ﴿They will not taste death therein, except the first death﴾ mean: except the tasting that results from remembering the first death.

The second question: Do not the people of Hell also not die? Why then did He give the people of Paradise good news of this, when the people of Hell share it with them? The answer: the good news was not given by the continuation of life alone, but by the continuation of life together with the prior attainment of those good things and felicities, so the difference is clear.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿and He protected them from the punishment of the Blazing Fire﴾. It was read as "wa-waqqahum" with shadda. If they say: the logical order would be for the mention of protection from the punishment of the Blazing Fire to precede the mention of triumph with Paradise, because one who is protected from the punishment of the Blazing Fire may or may not triumph; so when it is mentioned after that that he has triumphed with Paradise, the benefit is achieved. As for one who has attained the good things of Paradise, he has certainly been freed from the punishment of Allah, so mentioning triumph over the punishment of Hell after triumph with the reward of Paradise would not be beneficial. We say: the meaning is as if He, the Exalted, said: "and He protected them at the first matter from the punishment of the Blazing Fire."

* * *

Then He said: ﴿as a bounty from your Lord﴾, meaning that everything the God-fearing have reached of deliverance from the Fire and triumph with Paradise comes only by the bounty of Allah. Our companions used this verse as evidence that reward is given as a favor from Allah the Exalted, not by way of entitlement, because when He enumerated the kinds of reward for the God-fearing, He made clear that they were all attained only by way of Allah's bounty and beneficence. The judge (al-Qadi 'Abd al-Jabbar) said: most of these things, although they deserved them by their deeds, are by the bounty of Allah, because He graciously imposed the obligations, and His purpose in them was to bring them to this station; so it is like one who gives another money so that he may acquire an estate, and it is said of that estate: it is from his bounty. We say: your doctrine is that this reward is a binding right upon Allah, and that if He failed to give it He would become foolish and would be removed from divinity; so how can such a thing be described as a bounty from Allah the Exalted?

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿That is the supreme triumph.﴾ Our companions used this verse as evidence that bounty is of a higher rank than the deserved reward, for He described it as being a bounty from Allah, then described the bounty from Allah as being a supreme triumph. This is also indicated by the fact that when a mighty king gives a hired worker his wage and then bestows a robe of honor upon another person, that robe of honor is of higher status than the giving of that wage. When Allah the Exalted had explained the proofs and clarified the promise and the threat, He said: ﴿So We have made it easy in your tongue, that they may be reminded.﴾ The meaning is that He, the Exalted, described the Qur'an at the beginning of this surah as a clear Book, abundant in clarification and benefit, and mentioned at its conclusion what confirms this, saying: indeed that clear Book, abundant in benefit, We have made it easy only in your tongue, that is, We sent it down in Arabic in your language, ﴿that they may be reminded﴾. The judge said: this indicates that He wants faith and knowledge from all, and that He does not want disbelief from anyone. Our companions answered that the pronoun in His words ﴿that they may be reminded﴾ refers to specific groups of people, so we take it to mean the believers.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿So wait﴾, meaning: wait for what will befall them; ﴿for they are waiting﴾ for what will befall you, awaiting misfortunes for you. And Allah knows best.

The author, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him, said: The explanation of this surah was completed on Tuesday night, at midnight, on the twelfth of Dhu al-Hijjah, in the year six hundred and three.

O Constant in Goodness, O Eternal in Benevolence, the radiance of the Throne and the light of the Footstool, the ascents of the heavens, and the lights of the fixed stars and the planets upon their stations testify for You, those that reach deep into the highest elevation, and their sacred ascents, far above the dust of the world of generation and corruption, that the First, the Eternal Truth, is not fitting for any of the attachments of intellects, the blemishes of thoughts, or the resemblances of created things. The moon, by its waning, confesses to deficiency; the sun, by the testimony of the ascents to its changes, acknowledges its need for the management of the Merciful. The natures are subdued beneath the overpowering power. So Allah is in the unseen realities of the lofty ascents, and the changing things bear witness to His non-change, and the successive things speak of the perpetuity of His eternity. Whatever we direct ourselves toward, that it has passed and will come, He is its Creator and higher than it; by His existence there is existence and bringing into being, and by His non-existence there is annihilation and corruption. Everything other than Him is lost in His majesty, scattered at the rising of the light of His dominion. Nothing in the intellects of creation reaches Him except that He is unlike all creation. To Him belong might and majesty, power and perfection, generosity and bounty. Our Lord and the Lord of our destinations, You alone we seek, and to You we pray and fast, upon You is our reliance, and You are the First Origin. Glory be to You, glory be to You.

The third category is their sitting in a posture of facing one another, and the purpose of it is the companionship of some with others. The particle "ka" here has two possibilities: it may be in the nominative case, with the meaning "the matter is so," or in the accusative case, with the meaning "We gave them the like of that." Abu 'Ubayda said: "We made them spouses just as a husband is paired with a husband," that is, We made them two by two. They differed over whether this word indicates the occurrence of the marriage contract or not. Yunus said: His words ﴿and We paired them with houris﴾ mean "We joined them with them," so it is not a marriage contract, and the Arabs do not say "tazawwajtu bi-ha" (I married with her), but rather "tazawwajtuha" (I married her). Had the meaning been "tazawwajta bi-ha," it would have been "zawwajnaka biha." The first: that it is safe from everything one fears and dreads, and this is what is meant by His words: ﴿in a secure place﴾. The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: "Maqam" with a fatha is the place of standing, and what is meant is the place, which is one of the specific terms that has been used in the general sense. O Constant in Goodness, O Eternal in Benevolence, the radiance of the Throne and the light of the Footstool, the ascents of the heavens, and the lights of the fixed stars and the planets upon their stations testify for You, those that reach deep into the highest elevation, and their sacred ascents, far above the dust of the world of generation and corruption, that the First, the Eternal Truth, is not fitting for any of the attachments of intellects, the blemishes of thoughts, or the resemblances of created things. The moon, by its waning, confesses to deficiency; the sun, by the testimony of the ascents to its changes, acknowledges its need for the management of the Merciful. The natures are subdued beneath the overpowering power. So Allah is in the unseen realities of the lofty ascents, and the changing things bear witness to His non-change, and the successive things speak of the perpetuity of His eternity. Whatever we direct ourselves toward, that it has passed and will come, He is its Creator and higher than it; by His existence there is existence and bringing into being, and by His non-existence there is annihilation and corruption. Everything other than Him is lost in His majesty, scattered at the rising of the light of His dominion. Nothing in the intellects of creation reaches Him except that He is unlike all creation. To Him belong might and majesty, power and perfection, generosity and bounty. Our Lord and the Lord of our destinations, You alone we seek, and to You we pray and fast, upon You is our reliance, and You are the First Origin. Glory be to You, glory be to You.
